article.title: Blessed Are the Peacemakers
article.author: Walter G. Moss
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In The Sermon on the Mount Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). In 2025, President Donald Trump thought he should receive the Nobel Peace Prize, and in a December 2025 interview with Politico, Trump said this, “I settled eight wars . . . I mean, I settled one . . . one that was going on for 36 years. Uh, I settled Pakistan and India. I settled so many wars. I’m very proud of it. And I do it pretty routinely, pretty easily. It’s not hard for me to do. It’s what I do. I make deals.” In early October 2026, he repeated his claim . He also stated that he “stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon” and that “Obama got it [an earlier Nobel Peace Prize], and he didn’t do anything.” He also quoted last year’s winner, Venezuelan politician María Corina Machadoin, “There’s never been anybody in the history of the Nobel Prize that deserves it more [than Trump].” Despite these words, however, the 2026 prize was awarded to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, a former U.N. human rights chief and judge at the International Court of Justice. Trump’s reaction, according to The Washington Post, was that he “should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t. This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such an [sic] disgraceful and embarrassing decision.” Related: Israel's Conscientious Objectors Stand on the Shoulders of Giants What the world needs now, however, is a leader who understands peace and genuinely wants it, not one who suggests war and is indifferent to the horrors of it, at least as they affect people of another nation. A dozen years ago, I wrote “Where Is the Passion for Peace? ” In it I cited writer and pacifist Wendell Berry’s Blessed Are the Peacemakers: Christ’s Teachings About Love, Compassion and Forgiveness . The question of “where” today is the same as it was twelve years ago. Note this is a different query than “Where Is the Passion for the Nobel Peace Prize?” Although Trump has displayed that, no leader who can write --as Trump did about Iran in April 2026--"a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.” No such leader can be considered a true peacekeeper. Especially one who expressed no remorse about U. S. participation in the bombing of an Iranian school in the city of Minab , which killed more than 100 schoolchildren. Or one who makes a deal with Russia’s Vladimir Putin for diesel oil that Ukrainian President V ladimr Zelensky says woud play into Putin’s hands and prolong the Russo-Ukrainian War , which has been going on for four and a half years, about as long as WWI. The combined casualties (wounded and dead) of this recent war are apparently well over one million people--and close to two million . For what this means, one thinks of the words in Ian McEwan’s novel Black Dogs (1993) about World War II in Europe, that it was “a multiplicity, a near-infinity of private sorrows, as a boundless grief minutely subdivided without diminishment among individuals who covered the continent like dust. For the first time he sensed the scale of the catastrophe in terms of feeling; all those unique and solitary deaths, all that consequent sorrow, unique and solitary too, which had no place in conferences, headlines, history, and which had quietly retired to houses, kitchens, unshared beds, and anguished memories.” One also thinks of what Kenneth Boulding once wrote , “Peace is ploughing and sowing and reaping and making things and . . . getting married and raising a family and dancing and singing and opera.” War, however, is too often the killing or maiming of innumerable loved ones, whether adults or children, and the destruction of homes and communities. Today, as we look at Ukraine, Gaza, Lebanon, Sudan, some of us can imagine “all those unique and solitary deaths,” and we wonder if leaders like Trump, Putin, and Netanyahu imagine them. We doubt it. They lack a quality necessary for peacekeeping-- moral imagination . It seems rare for such political heads of state to possess such imagination and empathy. One possible exception was Germany’s Willy Brandt, who from 1957 to 1972 was in succession mayor of West Berlin, West German foreign minister, and then chancellor. In his A Peace Policy for Europe (English trans., 1969), he wrote: “The will to peace and to reconciliation is the primary idea and the foundation stone of our foreign policy.” And in the lecture he gave for winning the 1971 Nobel Peace Prize, he said something similar: “This is precisely the time for me to clearly emphasize my principles: War must not be a means to achieve political ends. Wars must be eliminated, not merely limited. No national interest can today be isolated from collective responsibility for peace. This fact must be recognized in all foreign relations.” If political leaders seem too ready to go to war, perhaps we should look to private citizens or religious leaders for more readiness to avoid or end wars. Both Pope Francis and Pope Leo have expressed the belief, as Leo stated it, that “War is never holy; only peace is holy, because it is willed by God.” Unfortunately, not all religious leaders share such a sentiment. Yet, there are encouraging examples of private citizens seeking peace. Besides those advocates of non-violent approaches, like Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Jr., and former Congressman John Lewis, there are non-governmental people who even during our present wars seek peaceful relations with their nation’s perceived enemies. Two such are Israel’s Jonathan Dekel-Chen, the father of a man who was shot and kidnapped from a kibbutz in October 2023 and held hostage by Hamas for almost 500 days before his release; and Gaza Palestinian Jaser Abu Mousa, who in post-October-2023 Israeli airstrikes lost his wife, two of his children, and his mother. The two men are seeking dialogue across their political divide. ( “Dialogue,” as opposed to war, was also an important alternative to Pope Francis. ) As Dekel-Chen proclaims , “We don't have the luxury of leaving a better tomorrow to our political leadership, to ideologues on both sides. If we continue to wait for this or that political leader to lead us out and to put aside the mobilization of hate for political reasons, then Jaser's children, my children and now grandchildren will be in a very similar situation not too long from now. If we can find a way to have reasonable conversations about how we can make life better for our communities by defusing hatred that has plagued us all for so long,” then such dialogue can lead to peace. Abu Mousa added that although his pain and grief were very real, he learned “to point them at the right direction,” and he turned to advocating dialogue rather than war because of his two remaining children - he didn’t want them to inherit his anger. He believes that when Hamas attacked the Israeli kibbutz they did not see human beings, and when Israel bombarded Gaza, they also did not see human beings. Instead, in both cases, they “took the people as collateral damage or as expendable assets.” What is it with leaders such as Putin, Netanyahu, and Trump? Why do they lack the moral imagination to empathize with the people they see as only enemies?
